name: FTX

summary.text: FTX was a cryptocurrency exchange co-founded by Sam Bankman-Fried and founded in 2019. It filed for bankruptcy in November 2022. The SEC alleged that Bankman-Fried diverted FTX customers' funds to his trading firm Alameda Research. A New York jury convicted him of seven fraud-related counts in 2023, and he was sentenced to 25 years in prison in March 2024.

facts.claim: In November 2023 a federal jury in Manhattan convicted FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried on all seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. On March 28, 2024 he was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

sources.title: Sam Bankman-Fried sentenced to 25 years in prison for his FTX crimes

facts.claim: Bankman-Fried's philanthropic group, the FTX Future Fund, saw its team resign in November 2022 as FTX collapsed. The team said in a letter that FTX's leadership may have engaged in deception or dishonesty.

sources.title: Crypto giant FTX to file for bankruptcy, CEO Sam Bankman-Fried steps down

facts.claim: The December 2022 indictment of Sam Bankman-Fried in the Southern District of New York included a count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and commit campaign finance violations, alongside wire fraud, securities fraud, commodities fraud and money laundering conspiracy counts. Prosecutors alleged that political contributions funded by Alameda Research were made to federal candidates and committees ahead of the 2022 election and reported under co-conspirators' names to conceal their corporate source and evade contribution limits and reporting requirements. An indictment is an allegation.
facts.quote: He is also charged with conspiracy to commit commodities fraud, conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the United States and commit campaign finance violations, each of which carries a maximum sentence of five years.

facts.claim: On February 23, 2023 a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court added four charges against Bankman-Fried, bringing the total to twelve. News reports of the filing said prosecutors alleged he and co-conspirators made more than 300 political contributions that were unlawful because they were attributed to a straw donor or made with corporate funds, that contributions were made in the names of two other FTX executives, one directed primarily to left-leaning candidates and organizations and the other to Republicans, and that many were funded by Alameda Research. Prosecutors did not allege that recipients knew the donations were unlawful. Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty.
facts.quote: Prosecutors said the contributions were unlawful because they were attributed to a "straw donor" or made using corporate funds, often allowing Bankman-Fried to evade contribution limits on individual contributions to candidates.

sources.title: Bankman-Fried charged with hundreds of illegal campaign donations

Bankman-Fried used customer funds for campaign largesse, charges say

facts.claim: NBC News reported in 2023 that prosecutors charged Bankman-Fried with using money taken from FTX customers to make more than $100 million in political campaign contributions before the 2022 midterm elections, and that court papers and FEC data identified Nishad Singh and Ryan Salame as the straw donors. The Justice Department's own releases describe the contributions as more than 300 in number and 'totaling tens of millions of dollars'.
facts.quote: Prosecutors said Bankman-Fried used money he stole from customers of his FTX cryptocurrency exchange to make more than $100 million in political campaign contributions before the 2022 U.S. midterm elections. Court papers and FEC data identified Singh and Ryan Salame as the straw donors.

sources.title: Sam Bankman-Fried charged with using stolen funds for over $100 million in political donations
Former FTX Executive Ryan Salame Sentenced To 90 Months In Prison

facts.claim: On February 28, 2023 Nishad Singh, FTX's former head of engineering, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to six counts: one of wire fraud, three of conspiracy to commit fraud, one of conspiracy to commit money laundering and one of conspiracy to defraud the United States by violating campaign finance laws. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams said the crimes 'corrupted our politics with tens of millions of dollars in illegal straw campaign contributions.' The SEC and CFTC filed related civil complaints the same day. On October 30, 2024 Judge Lewis Kaplan sentenced Singh to time served and three years of supervised release.
facts.quote: Singh pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, three of conspiracy to commit fraud, one of conspiracy to commit money laundering and one of conspiracy to defraud the U.S. by violating campaign finance laws.

sources.title: FTX ex-engineering chief Nishad Singh pleads guilty to criminal charges

FTX chief engineer avoids jail time for fraud

facts.claim: On September 7, 2023 Ryan Salame, former co-CEO of FTX's Bahamas subsidiary, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to make unlawful political contributions and defraud the Federal Election Commission, and to conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business. On May 28, 2024 Judge Lewis A. Kaplan sentenced him to 90 months in prison, three years of supervised release, more than $6 million in forfeiture and more than $5 million in restitution. The DOJ said that beginning around 2020 Salame conspired with Bankman-Fried and Nishad Singh to make contributions in a way that obscured Bankman-Fried's association with them.
facts.quote: In total, SALAME and his co-conspirators made over 300 political contributions, totaling tens of millions of dollars, that were unlawful because they were made in the name of a straw donor or paid for with corporate funds.

facts.claim: In its sentencing release for Ryan Salame, the DOJ said he conspired with Bankman-Fried and other FTX and Alameda Research employees to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, using FTX, Alameda Research and an entity called North Dimension to transmit FTX customer funds without a license.
facts.quote: SALAME conspired with Bankman-Fried and other employees of FTX and Alameda Research to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, unlawfully using FTX, Alameda Research, and an entity called "North Dimension" to transmit FTX customer funds without a license.

facts.claim: The DOJ said the November 2, 2023 jury verdict found Bankman-Fried guilty of two counts of wire fraud, two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and one count each of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, commodities fraud and money laundering, after a one-month trial before Judge Lewis A. Kaplan; the listed counts do not include a campaign-finance charge. At sentencing on March 28, 2024 he received 25 years in prison and three years of supervised release and was ordered to pay $11 billion in forfeiture. The DOJ describes him as the founder of FTX and Alameda Research who misappropriated billions of dollars of customer funds deposited with FTX.
facts.quote: 25 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and was ordered to pay $11 billion in forfeiture

facts.claim: In an interview with YouTuber Tiffany Fong released on November 29, 2022, Bankman-Fried said he had given about the same amount to Republicans as to Democrats in that cycle and that the Republican donations were not publicly disclosed: 'All my Republican donations were dark.' He said this was not for regulatory reasons but because reporters would react badly to donations to Republicans. Fortune noted he had been the second-largest Democratic donor of the previous election cycle.
facts.quote: All my Republican donations were dark

sources.title: Sam Bankman-Fried says he donated just as many millions to Republicans as Democrats

facts.claim: On December 8, 2022 Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission citing Bankman-Fried's remarks to Tiffany Fong in a November 16, 2022 interview about undisclosed Republican donations, and asked the FEC to investigate and, if appropriate, refer the matter to the Justice Department. The outcome of the complaint was not found.
facts.quote: The Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) filed the complaint with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) on Dec. 8, citing comments made by Bankman-Fried in a Nov. 16 interview with Fong.

sources.title: Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried hit with campaign finance complaint over GOP 'dark' money
FEC probe demanded after SBF 'admitted' making dark money donations

facts.claim: At FTX's first bankruptcy hearing in November 2022, the company's lawyers told the court that one FTX unit had put about $300 million into Bahamian real estate, mostly homes and vacation properties for senior staff. A Reuters review of property records, carried by NBC News and CBC, found that FTX, Bankman-Fried, his parents and senior executives had bought at least 19 properties worth nearly $121 million in the Bahamas over two years, with deeds describing some as residences for key personnel; Reuters could not determine who lived in them.
facts.quote: one unit had put about $300 million into Bahamian real estate

facts.claim: In January 2024 the Delaware bankruptcy court approved an agreement between the FTX debtors, FTX Property Holdings and the Bahamian liquidators of FTX Digital Markets to sell the group's Bahamas real estate, reported as roughly 38 properties (other reports say 35) with an aggregate purchase price of about $222 million, each to be sold for at least 80 percent of a broker price opinion. The Tribune reported that the proceeds would not be sufficient to repay the $256.3 million owed to FTX Digital Markets. Protos reported the properties were bought by senior staff partly with customer funds.
facts.quote: a Delaware judge approved the sale of $222 million worth of upscale Bahamas properties bought by senior staff during FTX's heyday, partly with customer funds

facts.claim: The CFTC's December 13, 2022 complaint alleged that in or around May 2020 Bankman-Fried directed that Alameda be exempted from the 'auto-liquidation' feature of FTX's spot margin trading, so that Alameda's collateral could fall below required margin levels without triggering liquidation of its account, and that Alameda was the only account so exempted. The SEC's complaint alleged that Alameda did not segregate FTX customer funds but commingled them with its other assets and used them to fund its trading operations and Bankman-Fried's other ventures. These are allegations in civil complaints, not findings.
facts.quote: As a result, Alameda's collateral could fall below the requisite margin levels without triggering the automatic liquidation of its account.

facts.claim: In December 2025 the SEC announced final consent judgments against Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang and Nishad Singh. Its litigation release states that Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh, with Ellison's knowledge and consent, had exempted Alameda from FTX's risk mitigation measures and provided Alameda with a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by FTX's customers.
facts.quote: had exempted Alameda from the risk mitigation measures and provided Alameda with a virtually unlimited "line of credit" funded by FTX's customers

facts.claim: At Bankman-Fried's trial in October 2023, FTX co-founder Gary Wang testified that Bankman-Fried asked him and Nishad Singh in 2019 to write code giving Alameda Research the ability to withdraw beyond a zero balance to pay company expenses and to ensure Alameda would not be liquidated regardless of its balance, that he had reservations at the time, and that Alameda had withdrawn $8 billion by the time FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022. Wang, Ellison and Singh had pleaded guilty and testified for the prosecution.
facts.quote: Alameda "had withdrawn $8 billion" by the time FTX declared bankruptcy in November 2022, Wang said.

facts.claim: The SEC alleged that Bankman-Fried directed FTX to have customers send funds to North Dimension Inc., an Alameda subsidiary, to hide that the funds were going to an Alameda-controlled account. The CFTC described North Dimension as a Delaware-registered, wholly owned Alameda subsidiary that, on information and belief, deliberately did not have a name readily identifiable with Alameda. NBC News reported that North Dimension's website presented it as an online seller of phones and laptops at the same Berkeley, California address that housed FTX US and did not mention Alameda.
facts.quote: The SEC alleges that Bankman-Fried directed FTX to have customers send funds to North Dimension in an effort to hide the fact that the funds were being sent to an account controlled by Alameda.

facts.claim: A pleading on the FTX bankruptcy docket in Delaware, quoting a government sentencing submission, states that FTX moved from Alameda-named bank accounts to a North Dimension account at Silvergate Bank, which became 'the primary means by which customers of FTX.com onboarded fiat currency'; that Silvergate maintained 45 accounts for FTX affiliates; and that FTX-related deposits there totaled approximately $1.4 billion by the second quarter of 2022. The same filing says FTX credited each customer's internal ledger on deposit but the cash itself was not segregated.
facts.quote: the primary means by which customers of FTX.com onboarded fiat currency

facts.claim: On July 2, 2024 the SEC charged Silvergate Capital Corporation, its former chief executive Alan Lane and former chief risk officer Kathleen Fraher with misleading investors about the bank's anti-money-laundering program and its monitoring of crypto customers, including FTX. The SEC alleged that because of deficiencies in that program Silvergate failed to detect nearly $9 billion in suspicious transfers among FTX and its related entities, and that misstatements from November 2022 to January 2023 were made in part to rebut speculation that FTX had used its Silvergate accounts to facilitate FTX's misconduct. A complaint is an allegation.
facts.quote: Silvergate allegedly failed to detect nearly $9 billion in suspicious transfers among FTX and its related entities

facts.claim: To settle the SEC's July 2024 charges, and without admitting or denying the allegations, Silvergate agreed to a final judgment ordering a $50 million civil penalty and a permanent injunction, and Alan Lane and Kathleen Fraher agreed to permanent injunctions, five-year officer-and-director bars and civil penalties of $1 million and $250,000. The settlements were subject to court approval, and Silvergate's payment could be offset by penalties paid to the Federal Reserve Board or the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation in parallel actions. Former chief financial officer Antonio Martino, charged separately, did not settle.
facts.quote: Without admitting or denying the allegations, Silvergate agreed to a final judgment ordering it to pay a $50 million civil penalty and imposing a permanent injunction to settle the charges.

facts.claim: The SEC's February 16, 2023 complaint against Singapore-based Terraform Labs and its founder Do Kwon alleged that from April 2018 until the scheme's collapse in May 2022 they raised billions of dollars by offering and selling an inter-connected suite of crypto asset securities, including the stablecoin TerraUSD (UST) and the LUNA and MIR tokens, many in unregistered transactions, and that they misled investors about UST's stability and about a Korean payment app's use of the Terraform blockchain. The SEC's amended complaint put the resulting loss of market value at at least $40 billion. A complaint is an allegation.
facts.quote: led to the loss of at least $40 billion of market value, including devastating losses for U.S. retail and institutional investors

facts.claim: On December 28, 2023 the court found Terraform Labs and Do Kwon liable for offering and selling crypto asset securities in unregistered transactions. Terraform filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on January 21, 2024. On April 5, 2024 a jury found Terraform and Kwon liable for securities fraud, and on June 12, 2024 the court approved a final judgment of more than $4.5 billion in total, comprising disgorgement, prejudgment interest and civil penalties of $420 million for Terraform and $80 million for Kwon, with the SEC's recovery subordinated to investors and creditors in the bankruptcy.
facts.quote: the Commission will not receive any payments unless and until investors and creditors are paid in full in the bankruptcy case

The U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York said its liabilities exceeded its assets by more than $1 billion and that at its height it had managed about $25 billion in customer assets; the FTC's complaint said Celsius then had over $4.7 billion in user liabilities.

facts.claim: On July 13, 2023 the SEC charged Celsius Network Limited and founder Alex Mashinsky with violating registration and antifraud provisions, including over its Earn Interest Program; the CFTC charged Mashinsky and Celsius Network, LLC with fraud and misrepresentations; the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York announced an indictment of Mashinsky; and the FTC announced a settlement with Celsius including a $4.7 billion judgment suspended to permit the return of remaining assets to consumers in bankruptcy. Mashinsky pleaded guilty on December 3, 2024 to commodities fraud and securities fraud and was sentenced on May 8, 2025 to 12 years in prison.

facts.claim: Voyager Digital declared bankruptcy in July 2022. The FTC's complaint alleged that from at least 2018 until then Voyager had used promises that consumers' deposits would be 'safe' to entice them to hand over their funds, and the FTC said customers lost more than $1 billion in cryptocurrency when the company failed. A complaint is an allegation.

facts.claim: In October 2023 the FTC announced a settlement banning the Voyager Digital companies from handling consumers' assets, with a $1.65 billion judgment suspended to let Voyager return its remaining assets to customers in bankruptcy; the court entered it on November 23, 2023. The FTC also sued former chief executive Stephen Ehrlich, who in June 2025 agreed, with a relief defendant, to pay $2.8 million and accepted a ban on marketing retail crypto products. The CFTC separately charged Ehrlich in October 2023 with fraud and registration failures and later obtained a consent order requiring $750,000 in disgorgement to Voyager customers and a registration ban.

openQuestions: Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven counts that do not include the campaign-finance conspiracy charged in December 2022; only Singh and Salame pleaded guilty to campaign-finance offences. Whether the campaign-finance count against Bankman-Fried was formally dropped, and why, was not sourced here.
Singh's political contributions are given as about $8 million (OpenSecrets, as cited by news reports) and $9.7 million (NBC News); neither figure is recorded as a fact.
Trial-testimony passages (Gary Wang) came from an aggregated search result citing Axios and TechCrunch; the owner should check which article carries each quoted line.
Reports that Alameda's FTX account carried an 'Allow Negative' flag and a borrowing limit of $65 billion appeared without clear attribution and were not recorded.

All Deltec claims come from Bahamian press reports and a pending class action; no court finding against Deltec was found. The $2 billion 'secret credit line' and Tether-related allegations reported by The Tribune in 2024 were not recorded.

The brief says customer funds were diverted 'to cover margin calls, pay off counterparties'; the sources here say the SEC alleged the funds were used 'to fund its trading operations and Bankman-Fried's other ventures', and Protos says the Bahamas properties were bought 'partly with customer funds'. No source was found for the margin-call or counterparty purpose.

Time and Salon reported that federal receipts show Bankman-Fried's disclosed giving went almost exclusively to Democrats (about $40 million, second only to George Soros); not recorded because no URL-tied passage was captured.

The NBC News '$100 million' figure refers to a later superseding indictment (reported elsewhere as August 2023) that was not researched; the DOJ's own releases say more than 300 contributions 'totaling tens of millions of dollars'. The February 2023 superseding indictment is now recorded from the court docket, but no Justice Department press release for it was found on justice.gov; the Criminal Division case page and the CourtListener docket are cited instead. The S3 indictment text itself was not read.

Whether the SEC's December 2022 complaint against Bankman-Fried names Silvergate was not verified; the SEC's separate July 2024 action against Silvergate, which names FTX-related accounts, is now recorded. The date of the bankruptcy-docket pleading cited for the 45 accounts was not captured. Whether the court approved the Silvergate settlements was not checked.

The Terraform judgment figures (more than $4.5 billion in total; $420 million and $80 million civil penalties; June 12, 2024 approval) came from SEC pages returned together in search results; the owner should confirm which SEC page carries each figure. The sources differ on whether the Mashinsky indictment was unsealed on July 11 or July 13, 2023.
